items.title: House committee releases data showing Commerce approved over 879,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China
items.summary: The House Foreign Affairs Committee, led by Rep. Brian Mast, released export-licence data on Nov 19 showing Commerce's BIS approved more than 879,000 advanced AI chips for Chinese companies out of 3.4 million requested, covering Nvidia H200s and equivalent AMD parts approved between December 2025 and May 2026. Reported allocations include 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD; the committee flagged approvals for companies the Pentagon lists as Chinese military companies. Mast singled out Maginfra and New Matrix as suspected smuggling fronts. It is unclear how many approvals turned into shipments.

items.title: Alibaba warns new US chip-access rules may force it to cut its 20 GW data-centre target and capex plans
items.summary: On its September-quarter call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new US restrictions on Chinese access to advanced computing chips, including via overseas data centres, could disrupt Alibaba's data-centre expansion, and that its goal of more than 20 GW of global capacity by 2032 may be revised down, with knock-on effects for capex. Management said the rules could affect products and services in 2027 and that Alibaba will invest more actively in domestic compute and supply chains, with in-house Zhenwu V900 chips expected to enter mass production in early 2027. It reiterated a target of $100bn in external cloud revenue by 2030.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first major Chinese hyperscaler to quantify how the Nov 16 US remote-access rule could shrink its AI infrastructure build-out, particularly in Southeast Asia, and push it toward domestic chips.

items.title: Trump and Xi discuss AI in Shenzhen but announce no chip deal; trilateral with Putin yields a 'peace declaration'

Xi said the two countries should work together to keep AI 'under human control', while Trump said the US opposes 'globalist regulation' of AI in any form, though he cited a shared interest in safety. Neither side announced any change to US chip export controls or the new remote-access rule. The first Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced a symbolic 'peace declaration' pledging dialogue on nuclear risks, with no AI commitments or timetable.
items.why_it_matters: The summit left US chip curbs, including the just-issued remote-access rule, untouched, so pressure on Chinese AI compute continues.

items.title: Reuters: Meta staff flag its Muse AI agent mixing up users' conversations and exposing private data
items.summary: Reuters, citing internal posts and its own tests, reported that Meta employees worry the Muse agent is mixing up conversations across accounts. Staff described unsolicited messages about childcare requests, career advice and bank balances that were not theirs. Reuters also reported that Muse read Signal messages using permissions granted at setup, not through Meta's Connector tool. Meta said many of the flagged messages were hallucinations it had already addressed. Reuters could not establish whether the data was real or invented, and Meta declined to say how many such cases there were.
items.why_it_matters: Muse is Meta's flagship consumer agent, with more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, and cross-account leakage or over-broad data access would be a serious privacy failure for a personal agent. The report comes as agents get deeper access to messaging and financial data.

items.title: TSMC halts Chinese designers' 16nm-and-below orders without US licences; Samsung also pauses some shipments
items.summary: TSMC has told affected Chinese chip designers to halt orders on 16nm-and-below processes unless they obtain US export licences, Reuters reported on Nov 19, citing two people familiar with the matter. Its guidance generally limits them to 28nm and 40nm, provided chips use no HBM or advanced packaging, and the checks extend to orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or intermediaries. The change follows new Commerce rules that removed a compliance route under which TSMC could assess designs' technical characteristics. The FT reported that Samsung has also paused some shipments to Chinese customers while it seeks licences.
items.why_it_matters: This closes a foundry loophole that let Chinese AI-chip designers keep using advanced nodes, squeezing domestic accelerators as well as Nvidia imports.
key_numbers: Fallback: 28nm/40nm, no HBM or advanced packaging

items.title: Google adds computer use to the Gemini Mac app, running tasks in a background window for paid US users
items.summary: Google began rolling out computer use in the Gemini app for macOS, letting Gemini click and type across local desktop apps and websites to finish multi-step tasks such as navigating menus and filling out forms. Tasks run in an isolated background window with a live preview in the chat, leaving the user's screen and cursor free, and are started by adding @Computer use to a prompt. Users choose which apps it can use, can pause it, and must approve key actions; it pauses for logins and payments. The rollout is in English in the US for Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers aged 18+ on Apple Silicon Macs running macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later, and is not available in Europe or the UK.
items.why_it_matters: Google now ships a desktop computer-use agent to consumers on a rival's OS, competing directly with Anthropic's and OpenAI's computer-use agents. The background-window design is meant to fix a common complaint about computer-use agents: they take over the user's screen.

items.title: Nvidia holds back its quarterly 10-Q over Huang probe disclosures as legal exposure widens

Investor Bill Ackman has separately accused the board of rushing to judgment and acting against shareholders' interests.

items.title: Google opens Genie 4 world model to Gemini API developers at about $0.10 per second of streamed world
items.summary: Google made its Genie 4 interactive world model available to developers through the Gemini Interactions API and Google AI Studio, as a paid-only service. Reported token pricing is $1.50 per million tokens for text or reference-image input, $9 per million for text output and $17.50 per million for video output with stereo audio. At 5,760 video tokens per second, that comes to roughly $0.10 per second, or about $6.05 per minute. The free tier, Batch API, Flex and Priority inference are not supported, and billing continues for as long as a session stays open.
items.why_it_matters: This is the first public price for a frontier real-time world model, and it lets developers estimate costs for games, simulation and agent training built on Genie 4. At about $363 an hour of generated world, sustained use is still expensive.

learn.title: Turn a data-centre power budget into training compute and model size
learn.why_today: Alibaba says US chip-access rules may force it to revise its target of more than 20 GW of capacity by 2032. A power target is really a compute target, and the chain from watts to trainable parameters shows what such a cut costs.
learn.explanation: Facility power divided by PUE gives IT power, and IT power divided by all-in watts per accelerator gives a device count. Multiply by peak FLOP/s and model FLOPs utilisation (MFU, typically 30-50% for large dense or MoE training) to get sustained FLOP/s, then by wall-clock time to get a run's compute C. For a dense transformer, training costs about C = 6ND FLOPs for N parameters and D tokens, and the Chinchilla fit puts the compute-optimal ratio near D/N = 20, so N grows as sqrt(C). That square root is why a 40% power cut costs only about 23% in compute-optimal model size, though it costs the full 40% in throughput for inference. The chain breaks where its assumptions do: MoE models count only active parameters in 6ND, production runs are deliberately over-trained past Chinchilla for cheaper inference, and interconnect or memory limits can cap MFU well below the chip's peak.
learn.math: C = \frac{P_{site}}{\mathrm{PUE}\, W_{acc}}\, F_{peak}\, \mathrm{MFU}\, t, \qquad C \approx 6ND,\; D \approx 20N \Rightarrow N \approx \sqrt{C/120}
learn.python:
# From gigawatts to a training run. All hardware numbers are illustrative, not any company's.
P_site = 1e9          # 1 GW of facility power
PUE = 1.3             # facility overhead: cooling, conversion losses
W_per_accel = 1800.0  # all-in IT watts per accelerator (chip + host + network share)
peak = 2.5e15         # dense BF16 FLOP/s per accelerator (illustrative)
for mfu in (0.30, 0.45):
    n = P_site / PUE / W_per_accel
    flops = n * peak * mfu                      # sustained FLOP/s for the whole site
    days = 90
    C = flops * days * 86400                    # FLOPs in a 90-day run
    # Chinchilla-style compute-optimal split: C = 6 N D with D = 20 N
    N = (C / 120) ** 0.5
    D = 20 * N
    print(f"MFU {mfu:.0%}: {n/1e3:,.0f}k accelerators, {flops:.2e} FLOP/s, "
          f"90-day C = {C:.2e} FLOP -> N = {N/1e12:.1f}T params, D = {D/1e12:.0f}T tokens")
# Same site, but only 60% of the planned power is built (a cut target):
print("power cut to 60% scales C by 0.6 and compute-optimal N by", round(0.6**0.5, 3))

learn.title: Scope every agent cache, memory and credential to the principal
learn.why_today: Reuters reports Meta staff saw the Muse agent surface messages from other people's accounts, which Meta says were mostly hallucinations. Whatever the cause there, cross-account bleed is a classic failure mode worth designing out as agents like Gemini's new Mac computer use gain access to personal data.
learn.explanation: An agent has more shared state than a chatbot: response and tool-result caches, long-term memory stores, retrieval indexes, and the credentials its tools use. If any of these is keyed on content alone (the prompt, a URL, a query embedding), two users who send the same request can receive each other's results, because the output depended on who asked but the key did not. The fix is to treat the principal (user, tenant, session) as part of every key and every row, to filter retrieval by principal before ranking rather than after, and to mint tool credentials per principal with least privilege, so a confused agent cannot read what its token cannot reach. Caching stays safe for genuinely public, user-independent results, but that must be an explicit decision. Tests should replay identical requests from two principals and assert that their outputs share nothing private.

learn.title: Estimate serving cost per token from memory bandwidth and batch size
learn.why_today: Alibaba blamed the widening RMB10.5bn loss in the segment that houses Qwen partly on Qwen app inference costs. The cost of a consumer chatbot comes down to how many tokens each accelerator-hour produces.
learn.explanation: In autoregressive decoding each step produces one token per sequence but must stream all active weights from HBM, plus each sequence's KV cache. At batch 1 the arithmetic units sit idle and throughput is roughly bandwidth / weight bytes, so decode is memory-bound. Batching amortises the weight read across sequences, so tokens per second rise almost linearly at first. That is why providers batch aggressively and why free consumer traffic with long contexts is expensive. The KV term grows with batch times context, so it eventually dominates and throughput saturates. That is the motivation for grouped-query or multi-head latent attention, KV quantisation, and paged KV memory. The model ignores prefill (compute-bound), latency targets that cap batch size, and speculative decoding; treat it as a first-order bound, not a price quote.
learn.math: \text{tok/s} \approx B\, \frac{BW}{N_{act} b_w + B\, T\, m_{KV}}, \qquad \$/\text{M tok} = \frac{10^6\, p_{hr}}{3600\, \text{tok/s}}
learn.python:
# Why serving a chat app costs real money: decode is memory-bandwidth bound.
# Illustrative numbers only; not any vendor's model or GPU.
HBM = 4.0e12          # bytes/s of memory bandwidth per accelerator
gpu_hour = 3.0        # $ per accelerator-hour
active = 30e9         # active params per token (an MoE's activated experts)
bytes_per_w = 1       # FP8 weights
kv_per_tok = 70e3     # KV-cache bytes per token of context (layers x heads x dim x 2 x bytes)
ctx = 8000            # tokens of context per sequence
for batch in (1, 16, 128):
    # each decode step streams the weights once (shared by the batch) + each sequence's KV cache
    bytes_step = active * bytes_per_w + batch * ctx * kv_per_tok
    steps = HBM / bytes_step                      # decode steps per second
    tok_s = steps * batch
    cost = gpu_hour / (tok_s * 3600) * 1e6        # $ per million output tokens
    print(f"batch {batch:4d}: {tok_s:8.0f} tok/s, ${cost:7.2f} per M output tokens")
